Deinosuchus.Name: Deinosuchus
Deinosuchus.Size: Adults have been found to be over 35 ft!
Deinosuchus.FunFact: Fossils of Deinosuchus were first found in North Carolina. Growth rings in the fossil bones suggest they could live over 50 years, and the biggest individuals are estimated to have been over 30 feet long, making them dangerous to even the dinosaurs they lived alongside.

Giant Ground Sloth.Name: Giant Ground Sloth
Giant Ground Sloth.FunFact: Megalonyx jeffersoni, a giant relative of today's tree sloths, is named after former U.S. President Thomas Jefferson. He discovered a fossil of the "great claw" in Virginia and mistakenly believed it to be from a massive tiger-like cat.

Bootherium Bombifrons.Name: Woodland Muskox
Bootherium Bombifrons.FunFact: Unlike their modern tundra muskox relatives, Bootherium lived in less cold, forested environments, including in North Carolina. Males had gigantic horns which met and fused in the middle, forming an intimidating, helmet-like structure on their heads.

Mammoth Tusk.Name: Mammoth
Mammoth Tusk.Location: Africa, Europe, Asia, and North America during the
Mammoth Tusk.FunFact: Mammoths represent some of the largest mammals to inhabit North America, and thrived in grasslands. Wooly mammoths were frigid, cold-weather specialists covered in fur, while Colombian mammoths were mostly hairless but even larger.

Horse Teeth.Name: Equus
Horse Teeth.Location: North America, South America, Asia, Africa, and Europe from the
Horse Teeth.FunFact: Horses originally evolved in North America. The first horses were small, three-toed forest dwellers, but eventually evolved into larger, single-toed plains animals. Their tall, evergrowing teeth are commonly found Pleistocene fossils.

Otodus Megalodon.Name: Megalodon
Otodus Megalodon.Diet: Whales, Dolphins, Seals, Sea Turtles, and Large Fish
Otodus Megalodon.FunFact: Whale fossils from the time of Otodus commonly have deep bite marks from attacks by this shark. While frequently depicted as just a giant great White Shark, preserved vertebral columns suggest they were longer bodied, like living lemon sharks and may have reached lengths over 70 feet!

Mosasaur.Name: Mosasaur
Mosasaur.Diet: Small and Large Fish and Ammonites
Mosasaur.FunFact: Considered a small mosasaur at a length of 13 feet, Clidastes was still an adept underwater predator. It inhabited the salt waters of the Western Interior Seaway and Atlantic ocean, but still occasoinally visited freshwater estuaries and rivers to hunt and drink.

Xiphiacetus.Name: Long-Nosed Dolphin
Xiphiacetus.FunFact: Xiphiacetus belongs to an extinct group of dolphins with long, swordfish-like beaks. These long-nosed dolphins are common fossils in Miocene rocks along the East Coast and Mediterranean, but the purpose of their impressive beak is still a mystery.

Prinonchelys.Name: Prionochelys
Prinonchelys.FunFact: Prionochelys was an early sea turtle that lived in the waters along coastal Appalachia and Laramidia. Prominent spikes and ridges on the edges of this turtle's shell may have helped protect them from sharks, large predatory fish, mosasaurs and pliosaurs that they lived alongside.

Plesiosaur.Name: Plesiosaur
Plesiosaur.FunFact: These long necked, nearly 40 foot marine reptiles inhabited shallower waters close to shore. Many fossils contain swallowed, rounded river pebbles called gastroliths. These were likely ingested to help break down the bones and shells of their prey.

Hadrosaur Jaw.Name: High-Crested Duckbill
Hadrosaur Jaw.FunFact: Hypacrosaurus is a crested duck-billed dinosaur. An amazing hatchling specimen from Montana is so well preserved that paleontologists discovered fossilized cellular structures from cartilage inside the bones of the fossil.

Grallator Tracks.Name: Grallator (Dinosaur Track)
Grallator Tracks.IsDino: No, but they're made by a dinosaur
Grallator Tracks.FunFact: Grallator isn't your average dinosaur fossil. It's a special type of fossil called a trace fossil. Rather than being the bones of a specific dinosaur, Grallator is specifically the fossilized footprints of smaller, theropod dinosaurs who walk on three toes.

Exogyra.Name: Exogyra
Exogyra.FunFact: These marine oysters frequently helped form shell-reefs in shallow Cretaceous seas across the Atlantic and Southeast coasts. These reef formed important habitats for other oceangoing creatures such as prehistoric sharks, marine reptiles and other invertebrates.

Helicoprion.Name: Whorl Tooth Shark
Helicoprion.Location: North America, Asia, and Australia during
Helicoprion.FunFact: Helicoprion is an shark-like cartilaginous fish most closely related to modern chimaeras. It is known for it's strange, spirally arranged tooth whorl which was likely a specialized device for hunting ammonites.

Crinoids.Name: Crinoids
Crinoids.FunFact: Despite looking like plants, crinoids like Solanocrinites are actually animals closely related to starfish and sea urchins. Crinoids still exist today, but tend to live in deep sea environments or only move around at night.

Diplocaulus.Name: Diplocaulus
Diplocaulus.Location: North America and Africa during the
Diplocaulus.FunFact: The purpose of the strange boomerang shaped parts of this early amphibian's head isn't certain, but they may have allowed Diplocaulus to rise rapidly in the water to pursue fish and insects. These animals were sometimes prey for the sail-backed land predator Dimetrodon.

Tiktaalik.Name: Tiktaalik
Tiktaalik.Diet: Their diet consisted of smaller fish.
Tiktaalik.FunFact: Tiktaalik is one of the earliest known fish with clear tetrapod, or four legged, skeletal adaptations. Paleontologists predicted what age and location of rocks should have such a fossil, and then later found it in the field!

Giant Sea Scorpion.Name: Mixopterus
Giant Sea Scorpion.FunFact: "Sea scorpions" like Mixopterus lived in aquatic habitats during the Paleozoic, and created the oldest known land footprints. Computer generated models suggest that Mixopterus trapped prey with it's larger arms, before impaling them with the smaller ones.

Terataspis.Name: Terataspis
Terataspis.FunFact: Terataspis is one of the largest trilobites ever found. It's spiky armor was probably for defense against early sharks and predatory fish. Despite it's size and armor, it may also have been prey for Jaekelopterus, the 9 foot sea scorpion that is the largest known arthropod ever.

Eldredgeops.Name: Eldredgeops
Eldredgeops.FunFact: Triobites inhabited Earth's oceans from the beginning of the Cambrian until the end of the Permian. Eldridgeops had a spotted exoskeleton, and more complex eyes that gave it better vision than many other trilobites. Some collectors still call it Phacops, which is a similar, European species.

Wiwaxia.Name: Wiwaxia
Wiwaxia.IsDino: No, these are way older than dinosaurs!
Wiwaxia.FunFact: This soft-bodied, but hard shell-plated animal is believed to be among the earliest known mollusks, the group containing snails, squids, octopuses, and clams. Despite looking so different, it possesses similar mouthparts and shell growth patterns to these animals.

Aspidella.Name: Aspidella
Aspidella.IsDino: No, these are way older than dinosaurs!
Aspidella.TimePeriodText: The Ediacaran period of the Pre-Cambrian
Aspidella.FunFact: Paleontologists still aren't exactly what Aspidella is. These small, disk shaped fossils may be the bodies of an organism, bacterial colonies or just the part of a larger animal that connects to the ground. The Ediacaran life forms, some found in North Carolina, are still a puzzling and exciting mystery!

Hallucigenia.Name: Hallucigenia
Hallucigenia.IsDino: No, these are way older than dinosaurs!
Hallucigenia.FunFact: This creature is so bizarre that early paleontologists weren't even sure which was was up, or which end was the head! Modern studies suggest that Hallucigenia's closest living relatives are velvet worms and waterbears.

Bothriolepis.Name: Bothriolepis
Bothriolepis.FunFact: Bothriolepis is a type of armored fish called a placoderm, which were some of the earliest jawed fish. A small relative of the mighty predator Dunkleosteus, Bothriolepis was instead a bottom feeding animal which sucked up food from the seafloor and relied on strong armor plates for safety.

Dromicosuchus.Name: Dromicosuchus
Dromicosuchus.FunFact: This small, crocodile relative had long limbs and a light body built for speed. Only found in North Carolina, Dromicosuchus was clearly a catlike predator. The first specimen was bitten by and found undeneath a Postosuchus, meaning that the speedy croc wasn't at the top of the food chain.

Gorgetosuchus.Name: Gorgetosuchus
Gorgetosuchus.FunFactTitle: The Armored Beast of the East
Gorgetosuchus.FunFact: Found only in North Carolina, Gorgetosuchus belongs to a group of armored, omnivorous reptiles closely related to dinosaurs and crocodiles. Named by Appalachian State University professor Andy Heckert, a life size statue of this animal can be visited on App State's campus.

Coahomasuchus.Name: Coahomasuchus
Coahomasuchus.FunFact: Unlike many other armored aetosaurs, Coahomasuchus' sharp teeth may have been primarily for eating meat. Different species of Coahomasuchus have been found first in Texas and more recently in North Carolina.

Swartpuntia.Name: Swartpuntia
Swartpuntia.IsDino: No, Swartpuntia may not even be animals.
Swartpuntia.FunFact: Swartpuntia is part of the mysterious "Ediacaran fauna," a group of precambrian organisms that are among the earliest "complex" life known. North Carolina is home to rare deposits of Ediacaran fossils. It is unclear whether fossils like Swartpuntia are animals, plants, or something else.

Xenacanthus.Name: Xenacanthus
Xenacanthus.Location: North America, Europe and Asia during the
Xenacanthus.FunFact: Xenacanthus lived only in freshwater environments. They possessed a single, sometimes barbed spine that pointed backwards from their head as a defense against larger predators. Their teeth were all split into two separate points, shaped like the letter "V."

Casteroides.Name: Casteroides
Casteroides.FunFactTitle: To Tree Or Not To Tree?
Casteroides.FunFact: Despite looking similar to modern beavers and sharing the same Ice Age habitats, Castoroides probably didn't build dams or chew wood. Their diet consisted of soft, underwater plants, and they had a longer, thinner tail than their distant beaver cousins.

Boreogomphodon.Name: Boreogomphodon
Boreogomphodon.FunFact: This mammal-like reptile is known from North Carolina and Virginia. They had more complex teeth than most other animals that shared their environment, making them excellent at chewing and processing tough foods.

Pteridinium.Name: Pteridinium
Pteridinium.IsDino: No, Pteridinium may not even be animals.
Pteridinium.Location: North America and Africa during the
Pteridinium.FunFact: Pteridinium is one of the strange Ediacaran organism fossils found in North Carolina. They had an unusual 3-way body symmetry with a canoe-like body. They incorporated mud and sand inside their bodies, and may have lived by absorbing nutrients directly from the water.

Postosuchus.Name: Postosuchus
Postosuchus.FunFact: Based on the shape of it's head and legs, Postosuchus was first thought to be an early T. rex relative. This archosaur is more closely related to crocodiles than dinosaurs, and would have been the undisputed apex predator of prehistoric North Carolina and Texas.
